title: Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents

details.title: Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents
details.abstract: Trajectory2Gym is a framework for scaling tool-use agents through compositional coverage and decision-grounded supervision. It constructs executable interactions that capture multi-step dependencies and trains agents on decisions supported by their visible interaction history. Across five Qwen3 model scales, Trajectory2Gym consistently improves performance on τ-bench, τ²-bench, and BFCL, achieving +16.9 to +29.8 percentage points in the average benchmark score.

title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent

details.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
details.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while overlooking implicit user intents (e.g., “where should I click next?” when a user is navigating a website) and fail to continuously update their understanding as user intents evolve. These limitations make them less suitable for intent-aware interaction in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark that serves as a testbed for user intent understanding and interaction, comprising 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with flexible lifecycles through hierarchical memory, enabling it to track the latest user intents and environmental states. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding capabilities while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over existing baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intents and determining when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation during sustained interactions, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction performance.

title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution

details.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
details.abstract: Task success does not always mean the agent harness worked reliably. We introduce TraceTrial-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates agent task performance and harness reliability separately, using 95 mechanism-oriented tasks across seven components: context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 3,420 runs, 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. Our framework combines trajectory tracing, multi-source evidence, and two-layer evaluation to support auditable reliability assessment and evidence-based failure analysis. We welcome feedback from researchers and developers working on agent harnesses, evaluation, and reliability!

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization

details.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
details.abstract: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.

title: Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL

details.title: Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL
details.abstract: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).

title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges

details.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
details.abstract: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.

title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents

details.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
details.abstract: 🚀 Introducing Continual Learning Exam (CLE): Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents! 🧠 Can LLM agents truly learn from experience and continuously improve over time? Most existing agent benchmarks focus on whether agents can solve individual tasks. But real-world intelligence requires more than task completion: agents should learn from past successes and failures, accumulate experience, and transfer acquired knowledge, strategies, and skills to future challenges. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate long-horizon continual learning and experience-driven self-improvement in LLM agents. 🌟 Key Highlights: 🔹 Built with 50+ domain experts, covering 120 real-world professional tasks, 600 progressive levels, and 89 occupations across 12 domains. 🔹 Realistic professional environments, featuring ~24K real-world files, 19 stateful applications, and 16K+ human-authored evaluation criteria. 🔹 Game-like Task Ladders, where agents must complete each level to unlock the next. Later levels require agents to reuse and build upon knowledge, strategies, and skills acquired through earlier experience. 📊 Key Findings: We evaluated 17 frontier agent configurations. Even the strongest system, Claude Code + Opus 5, achieves only: • 47.7% level completion rate • 23.3% full Task Ladder completion rate These results reveal a substantial gap between solving individual tasks and achieving genuine long-term continual learning. We hope CLE can serve as a realistic and verifiable benchmark to advance research on Agent Continual Learning, Memory, Skill Learning, and Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). 💡 Beyond Task Solving: Towards Continual Learning and Experience-Driven Self-Improvement. We welcome feedback, discussions, and collaborations from the community!

title: S3AC: Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic for LLM Reasoning

details.title: S3AC: Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic for LLM Reasoning
details.abstract: Critic-free methods are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, avoiding difficult and costly critic training. Common alternatives lack token-level credit assignment and typically rely on grouped rollouts to estimate prompt-specific baselines. A critic can address both limitations, but longCoT critic training is hindered by insufficient coverage of trajectories with diverse lengths and early gradients dominated by the newly initialized value head. We introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor–Critic) for LLM reasoning, built around a practical critictraining recipe. The trained critic provides token-specific advantages and prompt-specific baselines. Using the prompt-level baseline to estimate difficulty, we propose DifficultyAware Prompt Sampling (DAPS). DAPS combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing rollout waste without offline difficulty initialization. S3AC improves group-rollout performance across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 1.5B to 397B parameters, outperforming a modern GRPO variant (GRPO-X). At 35B, it sustains single-rollout training while tested critic-free baselines deteriorate after initial gains.

title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions

details.title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
details.abstract: Our contributions are as follows: 3D-grounded latent-action supervision. We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels. Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video. We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training. Representation and policy-level validation. We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data.

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We argue against the limitations of the traditional GRPO-type credit assignment, such as (1) the unreasonable reinforcement of unreasonable actions within the positively advantaged trajectory,  and (2) the fact that actions within the negatively advantaged trajectory are penalized with the same magnitude regardless of how much the remaining course deviates. Based on such insights, we propose ``ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning''.   It calibrates the GRPO-type credit assignment and results in the improvement of effectiveness and efficiency under multiple setups.

title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

details.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: 🚀 Can we really train LLMs with native FP4 reinforcement learning — without sacrificing stability? Excited to share miniTE , our open-source framework for stable and efficient native NVFP4 (W4A4) RL! One surprising finding: Same weights + same precision ≠ same policy. Even when both the learner and rollout engine use NVFP4, subtle differences in numerical execution can introduce significant training–inference mismatch and eventually destabilize RL. With miniTE, we tackle this challenge from both numerical and systems perspectives: 🔬 Diagnose & align: Identify cross-engine execution differences and bring training–inference log-probability gaps down to ~1e-8 in our strict-alignment setting. ⚡ Make FP4 actually fast: Optimize native NVFP4 kernels, scaling, and grouped GEMMs, achieving up to 1.39× BF16 learner throughput on 8×B300 GPUs. 📈 Keep learning stable: Demonstrate long-horizon RL on Qwen3-30B-A3B with downstream performance close to BF16. Beyond the results, we're releasing the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training recipes to make native low-bit RL easier to reproduce and extend. FP4 is not just about using fewer bits — it's about making every bit work. 🔥 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23928 💻 Details: https://infix.io/research/miniTE We'd love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and ideas for pushing low-precision RL further!

title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players

details.abstract: Excited to share our work, Build, Don't Play ! Can LLM agents build better game-playing AI systems than they can directly play? We introduce AutoTavern , a self-improving research system where LLM agents verify game mechanics, build a faithful Hearthstone Battlegrounds simulator, and iteratively improve a specialized RL agent through real-world feedback. In just 20 days, AutoTavern developed 23 versions of TavernAgent , reaching ~15,000 MMR on the live ladder. On TavernBench , our agent achieves 91% accuracy on play tasks (vs. up to 63% for frontier LLMs), making decisions in just 0.03 seconds. We also open-source TavernGym (a full-content simulator) and TavernBench (960 evaluation tasks) to support reproducible research. title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

details.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
details.abstract: Recent work shows that increasing embedding capacity can improve language models, making it a promising direction for scaling. As more capacity goes into embedding tables, extreme compression becomes increasingly important: we want to keep the benefits of larger embeddings while fitting models into limited deployment memory. We study this in Gemma 4, where per-layer embeddings (PLE) account for 35.2% of E4B's parameters. At 100× compression, only about five bytes remain for each token–layer vector. Encoding every vector independently gives each one a tiny code and misses the opportunity to share storage across layers. Our method, OPTIC, gives each token one quantized code shared across all layers. Layer-specific affine decoders reconstruct the different PLE vectors from that shared code. We also fit the representation to its effect after the gate and output projection, so the compression objective reflects how the model actually uses the embeddings. At about 100× PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% of BF16 E4B performance across seven benchmarks, compared with 66.3% for product quantization. Serving BF16 E4B directly from the compact codes reduces GPU memory by 29.7%, with at most 0.40% more wall time on an RTX 4090 with the same 1 GiB KV cache. It also works alongside backbone weight quantization. Paper · Code and method walkthrough · Released 100× PLE artifact

title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion

details.title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion
details.abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can synthesize visually compelling content, but maintaining geometrically consistent camera ego-motion across frames remains an open problem. Camera ego-motion describes these cross-frame viewpoint changes; geometrically inconsistent future predictions can induce systematic errors in downstream action prediction. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a framework combining causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment. First, we diagnose how ego-motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions. In the base model, both measures rise and then fall across denoising layers and timesteps: ego-motion is used at intermediate stages but is not retained later, a pattern we call geometric state forgetting. Second, we construct a delta-token space from a 3D foundation model and align VGM representations where ego-motion begins to fade. Delta tokens encode changes between consecutive frames, focusing supervision on motion rather than redundant static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign preserves visual quality while improving motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness. For example, it reduces geometric consistency errors by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, using the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves downstream world action models (WAMs) on the RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields gains in downstream embodied models on motion-intensive tasks.

title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters

details.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
details.abstract: Author here. Many LM pipelines end in a closed-set decision: pick a tool, a label, a route. We asked two things: how small an encoder for this can be, and whether it should read the options jointly or one at a time. Per-option vs joint: in a three-seed study at 32M parameters, per-option scoring wins by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps, and by 2.8 at roughly matched compute. The advantage needs a reranker initialisation; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Cost: per-option needs 5–13× more encoder passes, so joint is what we released. Released models: six open joint encoders, from 17M to 1B. On 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks, the 68M and 150M beat a 435M DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points. On the 145 tasks unseen in training they are at least on par with it. Latency: the 17M answers a median request in 14 ms on 16 CPU threads. A caveat we measured: reordering options changes 12–23% of the joint models' answers. Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/tardellirs/crivo-6acaa1731d71f839970f04a6 Code and results: https://github.com/tardellirs/crivo-decision-encoders Happy to answer questions!

title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents

details.title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents
details.abstract: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.

title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents

details.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
details.abstract: Ask an LLM agent to check the weather. It's polite, fluent and never says anything false... and twenty turns later you still don't have your forecast. 🌦️ That's procedural hallucination : the agent stops following the procedure it was given. Every turn looks fine on its own, so fact-checkers and per-turn quality metrics miss it. DialFork is a benchmark for catching it, with no annotation needed. We take a conversation where the agent does everything right, replay it with the same seed, and slip the agent a new instruction at some point, so the conversation "forks" 🔱. The fork position gives us labels for free: how far each fork strays and the turn where it starts straying. 36,278 English dialogues · 24 tasks · 12 domains · 4 hallucination types 3 tasks: set-to-set distance (monitoring), dialog-to-dialog distance (procedural retrieval) and turn prediction (real-time guardrails) 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/DialFork/dialfork 💻 Code & leaderboard: https://github.com/idiap/dialfork

title: Trust Mechanisms for Offline Generative AI at the Edge: A Connectivity-Regime Framework and an Empirical Study on a Raspberry Pi 5

details.title: Trust Mechanisms for Offline Generative AI at the Edge: A Connectivity-Regime Framework and an Empirical Study on a Raspberry Pi 5
details.abstract: We study what trust mechanisms do, and cost, for a fully local RAG assistant on a Raspberry Pi 5 running under network isolation (Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B/7B, 300 SQuAD 2.0 questions). Key findings: A calibrated retrieval-score gate detects out-of-corpus queries almost perfectly (AUROC 0.97) but in-topic unanswerable questions poorly (0.68). A simple deterministic output validator turns malformed outputs into explicit abstentions at no observed cost in correct answers. Signature and hash checks alone accepted 6 of 9 update attacks (rollback, replay, expiry, revoked keys, model incompatibility); layered verification rejected all 9 in about 4.5 ms. A validly signed but poisoned knowledge pack passed every check and eliminated correct answers on all 30 targets: integrity establishes provenance, not truth. Code, per-query outputs, and analysis scripts are open (DOI and GitHub links above); every table value can be regenerated with one command.

title: Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: A Case Study of GPT-6 Astra

details.title: Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: A Case Study of GPT-6 Astra
details.abstract: Can frontier AI models generate CAD models that are actually usable in engineering? Unlike evaluations centered on simplified or toy examples, our study assesses GPT-6 Astra using realistic engineering CAD models with nontrivial complexity. More importantly, we evaluate not only whether AI can generate CAD geometry, but also whether the resulting models satisfy multiple engineering usability requirements, including geometric validity, functional completeness, assembly feasibility, and parametric editability. Across CAD understanding, generation, editing, and evaluation tasks, our findings reveal an important transition: general-purpose AI models are beginning to demonstrate practical value in engineering design, while significant challenges remain in ensuring engineering reliability. The key question is no longer just whether AI can create CAD models, but whether those models can actually be used in engineering workflows. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24451 Project: https://qiang-zou.github.io/projects/icad-eval-report/

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Can Small Open-Weight Models Get Real Coding Work Done?

details.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Can Small Open-Weight Models Get Real Coding Work Done?
details.abstract: Most coding benchmarks measure whether a model can solve a problem. But what happens when we ask smaller open-weight models to complete real software engineering tasks? In Beyond Benchmarks , I investigate this gap through practical coding workflows, looking beyond benchmark scores to understand task completion, reliability, human intervention, and the economics of using open-weight models. The goal is not to declare a winning model, but to understand where smaller models are genuinely useful, where they struggle, and what it takes to make them effective in real development environments. I hope these findings help researchers and engineers building more practical, affordable, and accessible AI coding systems. Feedback, criticism, and independent replication are very welcome! Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34241
